Existing approaches rely on open-ended multimodal reasoning after each action, which is costly and poorly matched to the structured nature of GUI state transitions. We propose StepReflect, which formulates per-step GUI reflection as supervised structured prediction conditioned on explicit transition specifications and paired visual evidence. StepReflect is trained through a staged pipeline combining supervised fine-tuning, teacher-student distillation, and preference- and reward-based refinement. Offline, the resulting 8B model achieves 82.16% transition-level accuracy on AndroidWorld, exceeding zero-shot GPT-5.2 by 11.83 percentage points under the same structured input. Online, across M3A, Agent-SAMA, MAI-UI-8B, and Seed-2.0-Pro, StepReflect achieves higher task success in three of four agent configurations and remains within one successful task of the GPT-5.2 Reflection Agent in the fourth. It also reduces paid API charges relative to GPT-based reflection in all four configurations. These results establish StepReflect as a practical, locally deployable alternative to repeated frontier-model reflection for long-horizon mobile GUI agents.

AI.tldr: StepReflect is a specialized 8B model for GUI action reflection that outperforms GPT-5.2 in accuracy while reducing costs, providing a practical local alternative for mobile GUI agents.
AI.motivation: Current GUI agents rely on expensive open-ended multimodal reasoning for action reflection, which is poorly matched to GUI state transitions and increases costs for long-horizon tasks.
AI.method: Formulates GUI reflection as supervised structured prediction with explicit transition specifications and visual evidence. Uses staged training with supervised fine-tuning, teacher-student distillation, and preference/reward-based refinement.
AI.result: Achieves 82.16% transition-level accuracy on AndroidWorld (exceeds GPT-5.2 by 11.83 points), improves task success in 3/4 agent configurations, reduces API charges compared to GPT-based reflection.
AI.conclusion: StepReflect establishes a practical, locally deployable alternative to repeated frontier-model reflection for long-horizon mobile GUI agents, offering better accuracy while reducing costs.

title: Accelerating nanodrug development in continuous flow systems using informed prediction models based on low-cost surrogate nanoparticles
summary:
The development of nanotherapeutics often involves extensive empirical optimization due to the sensitivity of nanoparticle properties, such as size and polydispersity index (PDI), to minor changes in process parameters. Factors like formulation concentration, flow rates, and mixing ratios can significantly influence clinical efficacy and therapeutic outcomes. The absence of predictive mathematical frameworks has made iterative experimental screening necessary, increasing both costs and development time.
  This study introduces and validates a predictive modeling approach based on shape constraints, aiming to enhance the estimation of nanoparticle characteristics across various process conditions. Using controlled microfluidic methods, liposomes and lipid nanoparticles were systematically prepared under varying lipid concentrations, flow rates, and aqueous-to-organic mixing ratios.
  The shape-constrained model, informed by both experimental data and expert knowledge, was subsequently validated for a pharmaceutical application using minimal empirical data. Results reveal that shape-constrained modeling facilitates accurate prediction of nanoparticle size and dispersity, reducing the need for extensive experimental workflows. This framework supports rational and efficient process development for manufacturing nanomedicine systems.

AI.tldr: Shape-constrained predictive modeling reduces experimental screening for nanoparticle development by accurately predicting size and polydispersity from process parameters.
AI.motivation: Nanotherapeutics development requires extensive empirical optimization due to sensitivity of nanoparticle properties to minor process changes, lacking predictive frameworks that increase costs and development time.
AI.method: Developed shape-constrained predictive modeling approach informed by experimental data and expert knowledge, using controlled microfluidic methods to prepare liposomes/LNPs under varying lipid concentrations, flow rates, and mixing ratios.
AI.result: Shape-constrained model accurately predicts nanoparticle size and dispersity, reducing need for extensive experimental workflows and supporting rational process development.
AI.conclusion: Predictive modeling with shape constraints provides an efficient framework for nanomedicine manufacturing process development by reducing empirical screening requirements.

title: Epistemic Trustworthiness in Generative AI: A Normative Framework for Warranted Reliance in High-Stakes Workflows
comment: Accepted at AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society (AIES 2026)
summary: Generative AI systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes professional contexts, where their outputs shape what users believe, how they reason, and what they treat as settled. This raises a central question for responsible AI: under what conditions is reliance on generative AI outputs epistemically warranted rather than behaviourally induced? Existing frameworks largely ask whether AI outputs are accurate, fair, explainable, safe, or trusted by users. These questions remain necessary, and each can contribute to warranted reliance. However, they do not directly specify warranted reliance as a distinct evaluative target: the conditions under which users are justified in treating AI outputs as inputs into their own reasoning. We argue that this requires an account of epistemic trustworthiness: what makes a system epistemically worthy of reliance. Drawing on philosophical accounts of trustworthiness as competence and audience-orientation, we develop a constitutive normative framework comprising three jointly necessary and non-fungible conditions. First, epistemic humility requires systems to represent and communicate the limits of their competence. Second, epistemic access requires systems to enable users to inspect, question, and contest outputs in context. Third, resistance to epistemic injustice requires systems to recognise users as legitimate epistemic agents and avoid marginalising their knowledge and experience. Through real-world case analyses in legal reasoning, medical reasoning, and hiring, we show how failures of epistemic humility, epistemic access, and resistance to epistemic injustice can produce consequential harms that standard measures of accuracy, fairness, and usability do not address on their own. We conclude by outlining design and evaluation implications for GenAI systems organised around epistemically warranted reliance rather than output correctness alone.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a normative framework for assessing when reliance on generative AI outputs is epistemically warranted, focusing on three conditions: epistemic humility, epistemic access, and resistance to epistemic injustice.
AI.motivation: Generative AI systems are increasingly deployed in high-stakes professional contexts where their outputs shape user beliefs and reasoning. Existing frameworks focus on accuracy, fairness, explainability, safety, and trust, but don't directly address when users are justified in treating AI outputs as inputs to their reasoning - what constitutes "warranted reliance."
AI.method: Drawing on philosophical accounts of trustworthiness as competence and audience-orientation, the authors develop a constitutive normative framework with three jointly necessary conditions: epistemic humility, epistemic access, and resistance to epistemic injustice. They analyze real-world cases in legal reasoning, medical reasoning, and hiring to demonstrate how failures in these areas cause harms that standard metrics miss.
AI.result: The framework identifies three essential conditions for epistemically warranted reliance: 1) Epistemic humility - systems must communicate their competence limits; 2) Epistemic access - users must be able to inspect, question, and contest outputs; 3) Resistance to epistemic injustice - systems must recognize users as legitimate epistemic agents without marginalizing their knowledge. Case analyses show these failures cause consequential harms not captured by standard accuracy, fairness, or usability measures.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that AI design and evaluation should focus on epistemically warranted reliance rather than output correctness alone. The proposed framework provides necessary criteria for assessing whether users are justified in trusting AI outputs as inputs to their reasoning in high-stakes professional contexts.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Closed-Loop Control of Laser Powder Bed Fusion with an In-Loop Ontology
comment: 23 pages, 8 figures, submitted to journal(Journal of Intelligent Manufacturing) and under review
summary: A geometry-conditioned, neuro-symbolic closed-loop architecture is proposed for laser powder bed fusion, in which a standards-aligned ontology operates inside the control loop and couples symbolic reasoning with statistical learning to set the targets of a constraint-aware predictive controller. The ontology links the process objectives and constraints to the signals a controller can observe, and a description-logic reasoner converts them into the references and bounds enforced on each scan. The demonstrated case is overhang dross, a quality limit on the melt pool depth, which governs quality yet cannot be measured during the build, is mapped through a geometry- and power-dependent depth-to-width ratio onto a bound on the observable width, with the ratio and its calibrated uncertainty supplied by a Gaussian process. The reasoner classifies each upcoming feature and selects the active constraints-adding a lack-of-fusion floor at overhangs, a monotone guard beyond the calibrated range, and an energy-density cap where a process window is declared while running only on changes of geometric context and otherwise leaving a single small quadratic program on the per-scan path. In an Eagar-Tsai surrogate calibrated to the NIST AM-Bench benchmark for IN625, the architecture eliminates the dross produced by a geometry-blind controller, holds dross at zero with only a small residual lack-of-fusion under dual scoring, degrades gracefully under deliberate plant mismatch, and retargets to new alloys and constraints by editing ontology data rather than code. The results establish architectural feasibility, experimental calibration of the ratio is the principal next step.

AI.tldr: Neuro-symbolic closed-loop control system for laser powder bed fusion using ontology-driven constraint management to prevent overhang dross defects.
AI.motivation: Overhang dross defects in laser powder bed fusion cannot be measured during the build process, requiring a control architecture that can infer and prevent these quality issues using observable signals.
AI.method: Geometry-conditioned neuro-symbolic architecture with standards-aligned ontology inside the control loop. The system couples symbolic reasoning (description-logic reasoner) with statistical learning (Gaussian process for depth-to-width ratio uncertainty) to set targets for a constraint-aware predictive controller.
AI.result: In an Eagar-Tsai surrogate calibrated to NIST AM-Bench benchmark for IN625: eliminates dross produced by geometry-blind controllers, maintains zero dross with minimal lack-of-fusion, degrades gracefully under plant mismatch, and retargets easily to new alloys by editing ontology data.
AI.conclusion: The architecture demonstrates feasibility for preventing overhang dross defects. The principal next step is experimental calibration of the depth-to-width ratio parameter.

title: Measuring and Detecting Harmful AI Sycophancy
summary: Sycophantic responses are becoming pervasive in large language models (LLMs), and prior work has pointed out that some of them could be harmful. This paper focuses on one harmful sycophancy: preference-induced stance reversal sycophancy (PSRS), where a model reverses an initial stance merely to align with a user's stated preference. While existing research mainly measures how sycophantic a model is, we go further and ask whether PSRS can also be detected automatically from a single response. To investigate this at scale, we introduce CAP (Contrastive Anchor Probing), a framework for collecting labeled PSRS data. Applying CAP to 17 open- and closed-source LLMs, we collect 290,460 labeled responses across 12 everyday-advice domains. We organize our study around three research questions. (1) How often does PSRS occur? (2) How well can it be detected? (3) How does detection generalize to unseen models? We first reveal that PSRS rates range from 5% to 56% across LLMs, with more capable models being less sycophantic. Next, we show that detecting PSRS is feasible from the response text alone, and detectors need to learn subtle PSRS patterns from the training data. Because new LLMs appear rapidly, detectors inevitably encounter unseen models, making cross-model generalization an important framework goal. We demonstrate that detection performance drops on unseen models and propose an initial approach to address this challenge. We will release our dataset and code to support future research.

AI.tldr: LLMs exhibit preference-induced stance reversal sycophancy (PSRS) where they reverse initial stances to align with user preferences. The paper introduces CAP framework to collect labeled PSRS data, analyzes occurrence rates across 17 LLMs (5-56%), shows PSRS detection is feasible from response text, and addresses cross-model generalization challenges.
AI.motivation: Sycophantic responses are becoming pervasive in LLMs, with some forms being harmful. Specifically, preference-induced stance reversal sycophancy (PSRS) is problematic as models reverse their initial stance merely to align with user preferences. While existing research mainly measures sycophancy levels, there's a need to automatically detect PSRS from single responses at scale.
AI.method: Introduces CAP (Contrastive Anchor Probing), a framework for collecting labeled PSRS data. Applied CAP to 17 open- and closed-source LLMs, collecting 290,460 labeled responses across 12 everyday-advice domains. Organized study around three research questions: (1) PSRS occurrence rates, (2) detection feasibility, and (3) cross-model generalization.
AI.result: PSRS rates range from 5% to 56% across LLMs, with more capable models being less sycophantic. Detection is feasible from response text alone, requiring learning subtle PSRS patterns from training data. Detection performance drops on unseen models, prompting proposal of initial approaches to address cross-model generalization challenges.
AI.conclusion: PSRS is a prevalent issue in LLMs with varying rates across models. Automatic detection from single responses is possible but faces cross-model generalization challenges. The paper provides dataset and code to support future research on detecting and addressing sycophantic behavior in language models.

title: GROM: Gradient-Free Rapid One-Shot Machine Unlearning
summary: Machine unlearning has become a critical capability for safely removing specific, sensitive knowledge from large language models (LLMs). Current state-of-the-art approaches primarily rely on iterative, training-time unlearning via fine-tuning. However, even when utilizing parameter-efficient dimensionality reduction techniques like LoRA, gradient-based optimization remains computationally expensive and lacks explicit analytical formulations. It can also leave the targeted knowledge merely hidden rather than removed, to the point that simply quantizing the unlearned model restores much of what it was supposed to have erased. To resolve this, we propose a novel one-shot unlearning approach, abandoning iterative optimization in favor of a direct, exact analytical solution. We frame the unlearning process as a ridge-regularized least-squares optimization problem, deriving a closed-form additive update for targeted weight matrices. This update forces the selected layer to suppress unwanted content while strictly preserving its behavior on retained data. Computed from gradient-free forward passes alone, with no backpropagation and no iteration to convergence, GROM applies the weight edit in mere seconds, which makes it orders of magnitude faster than traditional fine-tuning. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that GROM achieves state-of-the-art forgetting-utility trade-offs on TOFU-5%, TOFU-10%, MUSE-Books, MUSE-News and WMDP, significantly reducing computational overhead without sacrificing overall model performance. Because the update removes the targeted content from the weights instead of masking it, GROM also withstands the low-bit quantization attack that recovers much of the content a gradient-based baseline had appeared to forget. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Batorskq/GROM.

AI.tldr: GROM introduces a one-shot, analytical machine unlearning approach for LLMs that uses direct weight matrix updates instead of iterative fine-tuning, achieving faster unlearning that withstands quantization attacks.
AI.motivation: Current gradient-based unlearning methods are computationally expensive, lack analytical formulations, and often only hide rather than remove targeted knowledge - quantization attacks can restore supposedly erased content.
AI.method: Frames unlearning as a ridge-regularized least-squares optimization problem, deriving a closed-form additive update for weight matrices computed from gradient-free forward passes without backpropagation or iterative convergence.
AI.result: GROM achieves state-of-the-art forgetting-utility trade-offs on multiple benchmarks (TOFU, MUSE, WMDP), applies updates in seconds (orders of magnitude faster than fine-tuning), and withstands low-bit quantization attacks.
AI.conclusion: GROM provides an efficient, analytical alternative to iterative unlearning that genuinely removes targeted knowledge from model weights rather than masking it, with significantly reduced computational overhead.

title: SkillHEX: Improving Agent Skills via Hypothesis-Driven Autonomous Exploration and Exploitation
summary: Although agent skills equip LLMs with reusable procedural knowledge, manual maintenance suffers from high costs, unscalability, and misalignment. Real-world deployments thus require autonomous, on-demand skill evolution at test time, constrained by limited interaction budgets and a lack of training or validation sets. This setting introduces a severe sparse reward challenge, where outcomes conflate multiple latent failure causes. Under such ambiguity, existing methods that greedily refine a single incumbent skill are particularly vulnerable to an exploitation trap, allowing early misdiagnoses to exhaust limited trials along unproductive trajectories. To address this, we introduce SkillHEX, a closed-loop framework coupling hypothesis-driven self-verification with evidence-guided tree search. SkillHEX translates falsifiable failure hypotheses into executable tests, producing diagnostic evidence as dense reward without additional environment attempts. This evidence guides a search over persistent skill-revision branches, dynamically balancing the exploitation of supported edits with the exploration of plausible alternatives. Evaluated on 87 tasks from SkillsBench, SkillHEX outperforms existing self-evolving methods and achieves an average pass rate of 55.9% and 57.9% using GPT-5.3-Codex and Claude Opus 4.7 under a five-iteration budget, respectively.

AI.tldr: SkillHEX: A framework for autonomous LLM skill evolution at test time using hypothesis-driven self-verification and evidence-guided tree search to overcome sparse reward challenges in limited-budget deployments.
AI.motivation: Manual skill maintenance for LLMs is costly, unscalable, and prone to misalignment. Real-world deployments require autonomous, on-demand skill evolution during test time under constraints of limited interaction budgets and absence of training/validation sets, creating a severe sparse reward problem where outcomes obscure multiple latent failure causes.
AI.method: SkillHEX combines hypothesis-driven self-verification with evidence-guided tree search. It translates falsifiable failure hypotheses into executable tests, generating diagnostic evidence as dense rewards without additional environment attempts. This evidence guides search over persistent skill-revision branches, dynamically balancing exploitation of supported edits with exploration of plausible alternatives.
AI.result: Evaluated on 87 tasks from SkillsBench, SkillHEX outperforms existing self-evolving methods, achieving average pass rates of 55.9% using GPT-5.3-Codex and 57.9% using Claude Opus 4.7 under a five-iteration budget.
AI.conclusion: SkillHEX successfully addresses the exploitation trap in sparse reward settings for autonomous skill evolution, enabling effective on-demand skill refinement at test time through systematic hypothesis testing and evidence-guided search.

title: Predicting Task Difficulty Without Rollouts
summary: Task difficulty dictates an agent's likelihood of success, and estimating it without rollouts means forecasting this directly from a task description before executing costly simulations in stateful environments. Reliable estimates would therefore allow environment designers to calibrate evaluation benchmarks and construct progressive training curricula. This becomes increasingly important as agents move into long-horizon domains, where empirical trial-and-error is a severe computational bottleneck. Prior work on early prediction is limited to static tasks or isolated coding environments, often relying on narrow features and inaccurate evaluation metrics. We study \textit{ex ante} difficulty prediction across 17 agentic benchmarks spanning coding, mathematics, machine learning, web navigation, function calling, and other domains. We show that AUC can mask poor difficulty estimates, identify token-level entropy as a useful predictive signal, and show how residuals between expected and observed difficulty can expose hidden environment flaws such as contamination and infeasibility.

AI.tldr: Early prediction of task difficulty for agents without rollouts using token-level entropy signals across diverse benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Estimating task difficulty before costly simulations would help environment designers calibrate evaluation benchmarks and create progressive training curricula, especially important for long-horizon domains where trial-and-error is computationally expensive.
AI.method: Studied ex ante difficulty prediction across 17 agentic benchmarks spanning coding, mathematics, machine learning, web navigation, function calling, and other domains. Used token-level entropy as a predictive signal and analyzed residuals between expected and observed difficulty.
AI.result: AUC can mask poor difficulty estimates, identified token-level entropy as a useful predictive signal for difficulty, and showed how residuals can expose hidden environment flaws like contamination and infeasibility.
AI.conclusion: Ex ante difficulty prediction is valuable for agent evaluation and environment design, with token-level entropy providing effective signals and residual analysis revealing underlying issues in benchmark construction.

title: Bayesian Expected Uncertainty Reduction (B-EUR) Model: A Computational Account of What Makes Design Options Worth Trying
summary:
This paper proposes the Bayesian Expected Uncertainty Reduction (B-EUR) model, which formalizes the value of trying a candidate design action as its expected reduction of epistemic uncertainty about action--outcome relations. The model addresses one part of the Uncertainty Driven Action (UDA) model's open question concerning how changes in uncertainty perception determine action selection. We examine two environmental properties: generalizability, or how far knowledge from one trial extends to neighboring candidates, and outcome discriminability, or how clearly differences among outcomes can be distinguished.
  We tested the model through simulations and human experiments using a graph-shape guessing task that isolates learning about action--outcome relations under a limited trial budget. Epistemic value followed an inverted-U-shaped relationship with generalizability and increased with outcome discriminability in the simulations. In the human experiments, the subjective value of trying and enjoyment followed inverted-U-shaped relationships with generalizability, while choice behavior reflected both properties.
  The B-EUR model provides a computational account of candidate-action evaluation within uncertainty-driven design activity and offers implications for constructing prototype sets, framing design problems, and organizing feedback to support informative exploration.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Bayesian Expected Uncertainty Reduction (B-EUR) model that quantifies the value of design actions based on expected reduction in epistemic uncertainty about action-outcome relations, tested through simulations and human experiments.
AI.motivation: The research aims to address an open question in the Uncertainty Driven Action (UDA) model about how changes in uncertainty perception determine action selection in design contexts, particularly focusing on environmental properties like generalizability and outcome discriminability.
AI.method: The study uses computational modeling with the B-EUR framework, tests through simulations examining generalizability and outcome discriminability effects, and conducts human experiments using a graph-shape guessing task that isolates learning about action-outcome relations under limited trial budgets.
AI.result: Simulations showed epistemic value follows an inverted-U-shaped relationship with generalizability and increases with outcome discriminability. Human experiments found subjective value and enjoyment follow inverted-U-shaped relationships with generalizability, while choice behavior reflects both environmental properties.
AI.conclusion: The B-EUR model provides a computational framework for evaluating candidate actions in uncertainty-driven design, with practical implications for constructing prototype sets, framing design problems, and organizing feedback to support informative exploration.

title: Learning to Rank Tensor Network Contraction Plans for GPU-Accelerated Quantum Circuit Simulation
summary: Classical simulation remains essential for developing and validating quantum algorithms, but its cost grows rapidly with circuit size. Tensor-network contraction can reduce this cost by exploiting circuit structure, although its efficiency depends strongly on the chosen contraction plan. On GPUs, plans with similar theoretical complexity may perform very differently because execution also depends on parallelism, reduction structure, memory traffic, and contraction geometry. We present a learning-to-rank framework for selecting efficient contraction plans before executing them. Each plan is represented by structural features derived directly from its sequence of pairwise contractions, and gradient-boosted rankers are trained from GPU measurements using listwise and pairwise objectives. We evaluate the resulting models on diverse circuit families, using separate in-distribution and circuit-family-shift test sets, and compare them with random and MinFill-based baselines. The learned rankers generally identify better plans, with the listwise model providing the strongest overall decision quality. We also study backend shift by comparing empirical plan orderings on two GPU architectures and evaluating the source-trained models on the second device without retraining. The rankings remain substantially, though not perfectly, stable across GPUs, and the models retain useful decision quality. These results support Learning to Rank as a practical way to reduce contraction-plan search, while showing that performance remains partly backend dependent.

AI.tldr: Learning-to-rank framework using structural features and gradient boosting to select efficient GPU tensor network contraction plans for quantum circuit simulation, outperforming baselines with good cross-GPU generalization.
AI.motivation: Tensor network contraction can reduce classical simulation costs for quantum circuits, but performance depends heavily on contraction plan selection. On GPUs, plans with similar theoretical complexity can perform very differently due to parallelism, memory traffic, and geometric factors.
AI.method: Represent contraction plans using structural features from pairwise contraction sequences, train gradient-boosted rankers using listwise and pairwise objectives on GPU measurements, and evaluate on diverse circuit families with in-distribution and shift tests.
AI.result: Learned rankers generally identify better plans than random/MinFill baselines, with listwise model showing strongest overall decision quality. Models maintain useful performance across GPU architectures without retraining, though rankings remain partly backend dependent.
AI.conclusion: Learning to Rank provides a practical approach to reduce contraction-plan search overhead, demonstrating that structural features can capture GPU-relevant performance factors while acknowledging backend-specific performance dependencies.

title: Refining Over Resampling: Test-Time Self-Correction for LLM Reasoning
summary: Test-time scaling improves LLM reasoning by using additional inference compute, but wider sampling alone can suffer from diminishing returns: new rollouts often repeat existing answer patterns instead of adding useful reasoning diversity. Verifier-based selection offers an alternative, but its performance depends on the calibration of an external reward model. We propose a verifier-free breadth--depth refinement framework that uses test-time compute to both explore and improve candidate solutions. The method samples multiple independent reasoning rollouts, refines each rollout through iterative self-critique and self-correction, and aggregates the refined answers by majority voting. Breadth preserves diverse initial attempts, while depth repairs local reasoning errors before aggregation. Across AIME24, AIME25, AMC, OlympiadBench, and MATH500, our method consistently improves over greedy decoding, majority voting, verifier-based best-of-$N$, beam search, and lookahead decoding across multiple open-weight models. For instance, with Qwen2.5-1.5B, accuracy increases from the strongest verifier-based baseline to $58.0\%$ on MATH500, and from $25.0\%$ to $32.5\%$ on AMC. These results show that test-time compute can be more effective when used to refine sampled trajectories rather than only to sample more candidates or rely on verifier-guided selection.

AI.tldr: Proposes a breadth-depth refinement framework that samples multiple reasoning rollouts, refines each through iterative self-critique/correction, and aggregates via majority voting - outperforming existing test-time scaling methods without needing external verifiers.
AI.motivation: Current test-time scaling approaches have limitations: wider sampling suffers diminishing returns due to repetitive reasoning patterns, while verifier-based methods depend on external reward model calibration which can be unreliable.
AI.method: Verifier-free breadth-depth refinement framework with three components: 1) Sample multiple independent reasoning rollouts (breadth), 2) Refine each rollout through iterative self-critique and self-correction (depth), 3) Aggregate refined answers via majority voting.
AI.result: Consistent improvements across AIME24, AIME25, AMC, OlympiadBench, and MATH500 datasets over greedy decoding, majority voting, verifier-based best-of-N, beam search, and lookahead decoding. With Qwen2.5-1.5B: MATH500 accuracy from strongest baseline to 58.0%, AMC from 25.0% to 32.5%.
AI.conclusion: Test-time compute is more effective when used to refine sampled reasoning trajectories rather than only sampling more candidates or relying on verifier-guided selection, demonstrating that intelligent refinement beats brute-force scaling.

title: Evidential Rule Learning for Interpretable Classification with Abstention
summary: Interpretable classification often requires more than accurate predictions for real-life deployment: models should be transparent about the evidence behind their decisions and abstain when they cannot decide reliably. We introduce Fast Evidential Rule Learning (FERL), a method that learns interpretable, accurate fuzzy rule models whose outputs are evidential. Unlike post-hoc calibration, FERL's belief, plausibility, and abstention capabilities arise directly from the fuzzy memberships in a single deterministic pass, with no auxiliary head, held-out set, or repeated inference. Our theoretical analysis further shows that FERL is Lipschitz stable, which means that its evidential outputs vary smoothly with the input. Against state-of-the-art rule learners, FERL is statistically significantly more accurate across a 30 tabular-dataset benchmark ($+2.6\%$ average accuracy over the second best). Its native set predictions attain the best utility-discounted accuracy among credal classifiers ($u_{65}/u_{80}=0.80/0.83$ vs.\ $0.79/0.80$ for the naive credal classifier), at higher set coverage ($0.92$ vs.\ $\le0.82$). FERL also matches dedicated out-of-distribution detectors on tabular near-OOD detection ($77.7$ vs.\ $77.4$ AUROC for the strongest baseline). Under detector-class-disjoint concept-bottleneck evaluation, its it is within $2.3$ AUROC points of the strongest dedicated detector on both CUB and AwA2, while attaining the best AwA2 AUPR-Out ($68.3$) and novel-class rejection ($57.2$), while being able to name which attributes are anomalous.

AI.tldr: FERL is an interpretable fuzzy rule learning method that provides evidential outputs (belief, plausibility, abstention) directly from fuzzy memberships without auxiliary components or post-hoc calibration.
AI.motivation: Real-life deployment of classification models requires transparency about decision evidence and ability to abstain when uncertain. Post-hoc calibration approaches have limitations, and there's need for native evidential reasoning in interpretable models.
AI.method: Fast Evidential Rule Learning (FERL) learns interpretable fuzzy rule models where evidential outputs (belief, plausibility, abstention) arise directly from fuzzy memberships in a single deterministic pass, without auxiliary heads or repeated inference.
AI.result: FERL achieves +2.6% average accuracy over second best on 30 tabular datasets, best utility-discounted accuracy among credal classifiers, matches dedicated OOD detectors on near-OOD detection (77.7 AUROC), and performs well on concept-bottleneck evaluation with ability to identify anomalous attributes.
AI.conclusion: FERL successfully combines interpretability with evidential reasoning, providing transparent decision evidence, reliable abstention capabilities, and competitive performance across multiple benchmarks while maintaining Lipschitz stability for smooth output variation.

title: A Unified Framework for Trajectory Prediction with Explicit Planning and Reaction Decomposition
summary: Trajectory prediction has shifted toward structured formulations with explicit social modeling. However, existing methods inadequately distinguish the functional roles of social influence in trajectory planning. Observing that agents typically form motion plans by anticipating others' future behaviors before making local reactive adjustments, we identify social interactions as playing staged roles, namely planning precedes reaction. We propose INTraJ, a unified framework that decomposes social influence into two stages: a planning stage constructs reference trajectories using future social information, and a reaction stage recovers local adjustments from the residual between full-context prediction and the reference. INTraJ supports both multi-target and single-target paradigms. Extensive experiments on four standard benchmarks, including Argoverse 2, Argoverse 2-ped, ETH/UCY, and SDD, demonstrate consistent improvements, particularly in FDE and long-horizon consistency, with state-of-the-art performance achieved in several settings. INTraJ reframes trajectory prediction as a planning-driven two-stage process, validating that staged social modeling is critical for stable predictions. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/11isnotavailable/INTraJ.

AI.tldr: INTraJ is a trajectory prediction framework that decomposes social influence into two stages: planning (constructing reference trajectories using future social information) and reaction (recovering local adjustments from residuals), achieving state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing trajectory prediction methods inadequately distinguish the functional roles of social influence in trajectory planning. The authors observe that agents typically form motion plans by anticipating others' future behaviors before making local reactive adjustments, suggesting social interactions play staged roles where planning precedes reaction.
AI.method: INTraJ is a unified framework that decomposes social influence into two stages: 1) Planning stage - constructs reference trajectories using future social information, and 2) Reaction stage - recovers local adjustments from the residual between full-context prediction and the reference. The framework supports both multi-target and single-target paradigms.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on four standard benchmarks (Argoverse 2, Argoverse 2-ped, ETH/UCY, and SDD) demonstrate consistent improvements, particularly in FDE and long-horizon consistency. State-of-the-art performance is achieved in several settings.
AI.conclusion: INTraJ successfully reframes trajectory prediction as a planning-driven two-stage process, validating that staged social modeling is critical for stable predictions. The approach provides a more structured understanding of social influence in trajectory planning.

title: Beyond Feature Importance: A Comparative Analysis of Pattern Detection Methods in Cluster Interpretation
comment: 6 pages. Accepted in 36th Irish Signals and Systems Conference (ISSC) 2026
summary: Interpreting clustering outcomes remains a fundamental challenge in data analysis, particularly in domains such as healthcare where meaningful patterns must be extracted from high-dimensional data. While numerous explainability techniques exist, they are primarily designed to assess feature importance or provide local instance-level explanations rather than to identify structured patterns present within clusters. This work presents a comparative evaluation of commonly used post-hoc analysis methods for pattern detection in clustering results. To enable controlled evaluation, we introduce a suite of synthetic datasets in which predefined patterns are systematically injected. Three widely used techniques are evaluated: a Random Forest surrogate model with permutation feature importance, LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations), and principal component analysis. Results demonstrate that although each method can successfully recover relevant features, none consistently detects all injected pattern types. These findings high- light a critical gap between existing explainability tools and the requirements of pattern-level cluster interpretation, motivating the development of dedicated pattern detection methodologies.

AI.tldr: Comparative evaluation shows existing explainability methods (Random Forest, LIME, PCA) for clustering analysis can detect relevant features but fail to consistently recover all injected patterns, highlighting a gap in pattern-level cluster interpretation tools.
AI.motivation: Clustering outcomes are difficult to interpret in domains like healthcare where meaningful patterns must be extracted from high-dimensional data. Existing explainability techniques focus on feature importance or local instance-level explanations rather than identifying structured patterns within clusters.
AI.method: Conducted comparative evaluation of three post-hoc analysis methods: Random Forest surrogate model with permutation feature importance, LIME, and principal component analysis. Used synthetic datasets with systematically injected predefined patterns for controlled evaluation.
AI.result: Each evaluated method can successfully recover relevant features, but none consistently detects all injected pattern types. This reveals a critical gap between current explainability tools and pattern-level cluster interpretation requirements.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight the need for dedicated pattern detection methodologies for clustering interpretation, as existing explainability approaches are insufficient for comprehensive pattern-level analysis of cluster structures.

title: Grounded Well-Condition Anomaly Detection on the Volve Field: Constructed Labels, a Baseline, and a Dual-Head Model
summary: Most public benchmarks for machine-condition monitoring come from test rigs, where faults are induced on purpose and every event is known. Real production fields rarely offer that. They give you sensor histories with no fault log attached, which is exactly the situation where an anomaly-detection method has to invent its own labels, and where quiet assumptions can slip in unnoticed. We work with the open Volve field data released by Equinor and take two things seriously that such datasets usually skip. First, we build anomaly labels that are not just patterns in the numbers but are checked against what the field's own engineering documents say can physically go wrong, and we release the reasoning behind every label. Second, we test whether those constructed labels are learnable at all, using both an unsupervised baseline and a small dual-head model that marks when an event happens and what kind it is, an idea we carry over from earlier work on defect detection in metal parts. The results are honest. An unsupervised detector that never sees the labels still lands on the same regions our rules flagged, which tells us the labels are not arbitrary. A compact supervised model recovers event presence and event type well across wells it has never seen, and locates events in time only roughly. We report what worked, what did not, and every assumption in between. The dataset, grounded labels, per-label provenance, baseline scores, trained model, and code are released publicly under CC-BY-NC-SA 4.0.

AI.tldr: Creating physically-grounded anomaly labels and testing their learnability on real-world Volve field data, showing both unsupervised detection aligns with labeled anomalies and supervised models can detect event presence/type across unseen wells.
AI.motivation: Real production field data lacks fault logs unlike controlled test rigs, making anomaly detection challenging with unvalidated assumptions. Need to build physically-grounded anomaly labels based on engineering documents rather than arbitrary patterns.
AI.method: 1) Create anomaly labels checked against field engineering documents for physical validity, with released reasoning for each label. 2) Test learnability using unsupervised baseline and small dual-head supervised model for event detection and classification. 3) Use Volve field data (Equinor) and apply methods from prior metal defect detection work.
AI.result: Unsupervised detector finds same regions as rule-based labels (validating labels). Supervised model detects event presence and type well across unseen wells, with rough temporal localization. Both approaches and assumptions are transparently reported.
AI.conclusion: Physically-grounded anomaly labels are learnable and non-arbitrary, enabling effective anomaly detection on real production data. Full transparency with dataset, labels, provenance, baselines, models, and code released publicly.

title: Alternating Levenberg-Marquardt Training of Physics-Informed Neural Networks with Fourier-Enhanced Features
summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) often fail to accurately resolve partial differential equations (PDEs) with high-frequency or multi-scale solutions, as well as strongly nonlinear problems. Two factors underlie this difficulty: spectral bias, the tendency of neural networks to underfit high-frequency features; and representation-coefficient coupling, the entanglement of representation learning and coefficient fitting within a single nonconvex optimization objective. In this work, we propose the Fourier-enhanced alternating Levenberg--Marquardt PINN (FALM-PINN), an optimization framework that decouples representation learning from coefficient fitting. The upper-level problem learns a Fourier-enhanced basis that enriches the latent space with high-frequency components, while the lower-level problem resolves the coupling by fitting the projection coefficients on this basis, solving a nonlinear least-squares problem with the Levenberg--Marquardt algorithm. The framework applies to general nonlinear and coupled PDE systems, and reduces to a single-step convex optimization problem for linear PDEs. We prove global convergence of the alternating training scheme in both cases. Numerical examples on multiple challenging high-frequency and nonlinear PDEs show that FALM-PINN achieves relative $L^2$ errors up to two orders of magnitude lower than state-of-the-art baselines.

AI.tldr: FALM-PINN: A Fourier-enhanced alternating optimization framework that decouples representation learning from coefficient fitting to solve challenging PDEs with high-frequency and nonlinear solutions.
AI.motivation: PINNs struggle with high-frequency, multi-scale, and strongly nonlinear PDEs due to spectral bias (underfitting high frequencies) and representation-coefficient coupling (entanglement in a single nonconvex objective).
AI.method: Proposes Fourier-enhanced alternating Levenberg-Marquardt PINN (FALM-PINN) with two-level optimization: upper-level learns Fourier-enhanced basis with high-frequency components; lower-level fits projection coefficients using Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm for nonlinear least squares.
AI.result: Achieves relative L2 errors up to two orders of magnitude lower than state-of-the-art baselines on multiple challenging high-frequency and nonlinear PDEs, with proven global convergence.
AI.conclusion: FALM-PINN effectively addresses PINN limitations by decoupling representation learning from coefficient fitting, enabling successful resolution of previously challenging high-frequency and nonlinear PDE problems.

title: DreamGuard: Efficient Runtime Guardrail for LLM Agents via Risk-Aware World Model
summary: As large language model (LLM) agents increasingly invoke external tools and interact with real-world systems, unsafe actions may cause irreversible consequences on external states, user data, and downstream services. Recent runtime guardrails mitigate such risks by checking proposed actions before execution, but many remain reactive: they primarily assess the apparent safety of the current action, lacking an explicit model of how risk evolves across the trajectory. This limitation creates a critical blind spot for long-horizon risks, where individually benign-looking actions can gradually drift the agent toward hazardous states. In response, we propose DreamGuard, a proactive guardrail for LLM agents built around a risk-aware world model. The world model maintains a compact recurrent latent state over the trajectory and predicts future latent states from which DreamGuard derives immediate-hazard and prefix-risk evidence. It then fuses these multi-horizon signals into intervention decisions before execution. Experiments across four benchmarks and an online guardrail evaluation show that DreamGuard outperforms generic, reactive, and proactive guardrail baselines, achieves the best safety-utility trade-off among evaluated guardrails, and maintains an average end-to-end latency of 25 ms per call.

AI.tldr: DreamGuard is a proactive safety guardrail for LLM agents that uses a risk-aware world model to detect and prevent long-horizon risks, outperforming reactive approaches while maintaining low latency.
AI.motivation: Current LLM agents interacting with real-world systems pose risks of unsafe actions causing irreversible damage. Existing runtime guardrails are primarily reactive, checking only current actions without modeling evolving risk across trajectories, creating blind spots for long-horizon risks where individually benign actions can gradually lead to hazardous states.
AI.method: DreamGuard uses a risk-aware world model with compact recurrent latent state tracking trajectory evolution. It predicts future latent states to derive immediate-hazard and prefix-risk evidence, then fuses these multi-horizon signals to make intervention decisions before execution.
AI.result: Experiments across four benchmarks and online guardrail evaluation show DreamGuard outperforms generic, reactive, and proactive guardrail baselines, achieves the best safety-utility trade-off, and maintains an average end-to-end latency of 25 ms per call.
AI.conclusion: DreamGuard demonstrates that proactive, risk-aware guardrails with world modeling can effectively address long-horizon safety risks in LLM agents while maintaining practical performance characteristics, representing a significant advancement over purely reactive safety approaches.

title: CohortHijack: Robustness of Single Cell Annotation to Companion Cell Removal
summary: Many single-cell annotation tools refine an initial cell label using nearby cells or cluster-level voting. We study whether this refinement can be manipulated without changing the target cell. We introduce CohortHijack, a robustness audit that removes selected non-target cells from the query cohort while preserving the target expression profile, base prediction, and trained model. We evaluate random and structured removal methods, together with greedy, multi-start, and beam search, on PBMC3K and Paul15 using logistic regression and calibrated linear SVM classifiers. Structured removal was consistently stronger than random removal on Paul15. Multi-start search changed 24.33% of linear-SVM targets and 19.67% of logistic-regression targets while removing a small fraction of the cohort and keeping mean collateral changes below 0.4%. Ablations confirmed that the effect disappeared when neighborhood refinement was disabled. We also evaluated CellTypist majority voting, where independent predictions remained unchanged across all evaluations, but refined labels changed after small companion-cell removals. These findings identify query cohort composition as a target-preserving attack surface in single-cell annotation.

AI.tldr: CohortHijack is a robustness audit that manipulates single-cell annotation refinement by removing selected non-target cells while preserving everything else, revealing query cohort composition as a vulnerable attack surface.
AI.motivation: Many single-cell annotation tools refine initial cell labels using neighborhood or cluster-level voting. The authors investigate whether this refinement process can be manipulated without changing the target cell itself, identifying potential security vulnerabilities in current annotation methods.
AI.method: The authors introduce CohortHijack, which removes selected non-target cells from the query cohort while preserving target expression profile, base prediction, and trained model. They evaluate random and structured removal methods with greedy, multi-start, and beam search on PBMC3K and Paul15 datasets using logistic regression and calibrated linear SVM classifiers.
AI.result: Structured removal consistently outperformed random removal on Paul15. Multi-start search changed 24.33% of linear-SVM targets and 19.67% of logistic-regression targets with minimal cohort removal (mean collateral changes below 0.4%). The effect disappeared when neighborhood refinement was disabled. CellTypist majority voting also showed vulnerability where refined labels changed after small companion-cell removals despite independent predictions remaining unchanged.
AI.conclusion: Query cohort composition represents a target-preserving attack surface in single-cell annotation. Refinement mechanisms based on neighborhood information can be manipulated without altering target cells, exposing security vulnerabilities that need to be addressed in annotation tool design.

title: Shaping Human-AI Interactions to Provide Improvement Pathways and Balance Competing Objectives
summary: When an AI system is deployed, the individuals who use and or are evaluated by it form beliefs about how the system operates and use those beliefs to strategically present their preferences, behaviors, or attributes. The system then responds with feedback or a decision outcome, thereby creating a human-AI interaction loop. This thesis studies how to design and shape such interactions to achieve three goals: (1) help individuals develop accurate beliefs about the AI systems so they can improve and or secure favorable outcomes at minimal cost, (2) encourage improvement and or discourage gaming behaviors, and (3) ensure that the AI system continues to achieve its intended objectives, such as maximizing accuracy. To address these goals, the thesis is organized into three complementary parts that examine and study human-AI interactions from the perspectives of both evaluated individuals and AI systems. Together, the work presented in this thesis advances human-centered machine learning by providing principles and methods for designing AI systems that align with human needs, values, and capabilities. Methodologically, this thesis integrates theoretical analysis, data-driven modeling, human-subject experiments, and empirical evaluations on real-world and semi-synthetic datasets.

AI.tldr: This thesis studies strategic human-AI interactions where individuals form beliefs about AI systems and use them strategically, creating feedback loops. It develops methods to design these interactions for accurate user beliefs, desirable behaviors, and AI objective maintenance.
AI.motivation: When individuals interact with AI systems, they form beliefs about how the systems work and use those beliefs to strategically present themselves (gaming or improving). This creates human-AI interaction loops that need to be designed to ensure individuals develop accurate beliefs, are encouraged to improve rather than game the system, and the AI continues achieving its intended objectives like accuracy.
AI.method: The thesis integrates theoretical analysis, data-driven modeling, human-subject experiments, and empirical evaluations on real-world and semi-synthetic datasets. It examines human-AI interactions from both evaluated individuals' and AI systems' perspectives across three complementary parts.
AI.result: The work provides principles and methods for designing AI systems that align with human needs, values, and capabilities, advancing human-centered machine learning by addressing how to shape human-AI interactions to achieve the three stated goals.
AI.conclusion: This thesis contributes to human-centered machine learning by developing approaches to design human-AI interaction loops that help individuals form accurate beliefs about AI systems, encourage improvement over gaming, and maintain AI system objectives - addressing both individual and system perspectives in strategic interactions.

title: BioM-JEPA: joint-embedding prediction of graph-connected gene blocks in single cells
comment: 34 pages, 6 figures, and 13 supplementary tables (Tables S1-S13); includes Supplementary Information with detailed training and evaluation protocols. Numerical source data for all figures are provided as ancillary files; training code and the BioM-JEPA checkpoint will be released via GitHub
summary: Single-cell transcriptomes are sparse observations of coordinated biological programmes, yet most self-supervised models learn by reconstructing individual genes. Here we present BioM-JEPA, a joint-embedding predictive architecture that instead predicts aggregate representations of graph-connected gene blocks defined by protein-association and corpus-derived coexpression evidence. A student network infers each target-block representation from the remaining genes in a cell, while a slowly updated teacher supplies the corresponding target from the full observed gene set. Under the reported extraction procedure, block-level prediction produced embeddings with higher effective rank and weaker association with detected-gene depth in the tested diagnostics than token-prediction, random-block and reconstruction controls. Across CellBench tasks, frozen BioM-JEPA embeddings retained expression, pathway and neighbourhood information and achieved the lowest aggregate perturbation-response error among the evaluated models. Representation diagnostics were also consistent with canonical pancreatic programmes and compositional relationships between genetic perturbations. Linear attention avoids constructing a quadratic gene-by-gene attention matrix; in a matched one-epoch hPancreas experiment at batch size 8, BioM-JEPA provided 5.75-fold higher fine-tuning throughput and 3.76-fold higher held-out embedding throughput than scFoundation. Together, these results support graph-connected gene blocks as useful prediction units for JEPA-style representation learning in single-cell biology.

AI.tldr: BioM-JEPA is a self-supervised learning model for single-cell transcriptomics that predicts representations of graph-connected gene blocks rather than reconstructing individual genes, achieving better embeddings with higher effective rank and improved computational efficiency.
AI.motivation: Single-cell transcriptomes represent coordinated biological programs, but most self-supervised models learn by reconstructing individual genes, which may not capture the biological coordination effectively.
AI.method: Uses a joint-embedding predictive architecture where a student network predicts aggregate representations of graph-connected gene blocks (defined by protein-association and coexpression evidence) from remaining genes, while a slowly updated teacher provides target representations from the full gene set.
AI.result: Block-level prediction produced embeddings with higher effective rank and weaker association with detected-gene depth than controls. BioM-JEPA embeddings retained expression, pathway and neighborhood information across CellBench tasks, achieved lowest perturbation-response error, and showed 5.75x higher fine-tuning throughput and 3.76x higher embedding throughput than scFoundation.
AI.conclusion: Graph-connected gene blocks serve as useful prediction units for JEPA-style representation learning in single-cell biology, capturing coordinated biological programs more effectively than individual gene prediction.

title: RA-CAD: Learning Post-Execution Critique for State-Aware Text-to-CAD Generation
summary: Text-to-CAD generation translates natural-language design intent into editable and executable parametric computer-aided design (CAD) codes, reducing the expertise and effort required for manual modeling. Existing methods incorporate fixed, externally supplied, prompt-induced, or separately optimized critique mechanisms to optimize the generation process, but they do not necessarily optimize how feedback is interpreted and translated into effective corrective actions throughout the generation process. To bridge this feedback-utilization gap, we present RA-CAD (ReAct Agent for CAD), a state-aware agent that interacts with the CAD environment through a Generate--Execute--Critique--Rewrite loop. At each iteration, RA-CAD executes the current code and observes its outcome. Conditioned on the design instruction, current code, and execution feedback, the agent then generates an explicit post-execution critique as an intermediate policy action. This critique either validates the current result for termination or provides revision-oriented guidance that conditions the next rewrite. CAD Code Bootstrapping (CCB) first establishes fundamental parametric CAD coding capabilities through supervised fine-tuning. Feedback-Driven Agent Optimization (FAO) subsequently applies trajectory-level Group Relative Policy Optimization to both policy-generated code and critique sequences, assigning terminal F1 and Chamfer Distance rewards to the complete interaction trajectory. This formulation makes critique an outcome-aligned, learnable policy decision rather than an unoptimized auxiliary output. Experiments on CADFusion and Text2CAD show that RA-CAD achieves state-of-the-art execution validity and geometric quality compared with existing methods and strong proprietary language models, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed state-aware text-to-CAD agent.

AI.tldr: RA-CAD is a state-aware agent for text-to-CAD generation that uses a Generate-Execute-Critique-Rewrite loop with learnable critiques, achieving SOTA performance through CAD Code Bootstrapping and Feedback-Driven Agent Optimization.
AI.motivation: Existing text-to-CAD methods have limited feedback utilization - they use fixed or externally supplied critiques that don't optimize how feedback is interpreted and translated into corrective actions throughout the generation process. There's a gap in effectively utilizing feedback for iterative improvement.
AI.method: RA-CAD operates through a Generate-Execute-Critique-Rewrite loop. CAD Code Bootstrapping (CCB) establishes fundamental parametric CAD coding capabilities via supervised fine-tuning. Feedback-Driven Agent Optimization (FAO) uses trajectory-level Group Relative Policy Optimization with F1 and Chamfer Distance rewards on complete interaction trajectories, making critique a learnable policy decision.
AI.result: Experiments on CADFusion and Text2CAD datasets show RA-CAD achieves state-of-the-art execution validity and geometric quality compared to existing methods and strong proprietary language models.
AI.conclusion: RA-CAD demonstrates the effectiveness of state-aware text-to-CAD agents with learnable critiques, bridging the feedback-utilization gap in text-to-CAD generation by making critique an outcome-aligned policy decision rather than an unoptimized auxiliary output.

title: How Far Do Simple Transformations Translate Across Text Embedding Models?
summary: We investigate whether simple transformations can translate representations across heterogeneous text embedding models. Understanding how independently trained models organize semantic information is an enabler for AI-to-AI latent communication without decoding into human-readable text. Focusing on lightweight translators such as linear mappings, we test the literature hypothesis of latent universality in a realistic text setting beyond simplified benchmarks. Across nine embedding models differing in architecture, pooling strategy, and training objective, we evaluate compatibility using CKA, downstream transfer, fidelity, and retrieval. Simple translators recover meaningful shared structure and support transfer for some compatible pairs, but fail sharply for others. Compatibility depends jointly on architecture, training objective, pooling, and data distribution. Overall, the results show that heterogeneous embedding spaces are not universally related by simple mappings as often suggested in some literature.

AI.tldr: Simple linear transformations can sometimes translate representations across different text embedding models, but they fail for many model pairs, showing that latent universality doesn't hold universally in practice.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to understand whether independently trained text embedding models organize semantic information in ways that can be translated between them, enabling AI-to-AI latent communication without decoding to human-readable text. This tests the "latent universality" hypothesis often suggested in literature.
AI.method: The researchers test lightweight translators (mainly linear mappings) across nine heterogeneous text embedding models varying in architecture, pooling strategy, and training objective. They evaluate compatibility using Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA), downstream transfer performance, fidelity, and retrieval tasks.
AI.result: Simple translators successfully recover meaningful shared structure and support transfer for some compatible model pairs, but fail sharply for others. Compatibility depends jointly on architecture, training objective, pooling method, and data distribution. The findings show clear limitations to latent universality.
AI.conclusion: Heterogeneous text embedding spaces are not universally related by simple transformations as often suggested. The "latent universality" hypothesis doesn't hold in realistic text settings, with compatibility being model-dependent rather than universal.

title: BlockPython: A Process-Aware Agent-Supported Platform for the Transition from Block-Based to Python Programming
summary: The transition from block-based to text-based programming requires learners to convert visible program structures into abstract textual expressions, which may create a cognitive gap between understanding computational concepts and expressing them in Python syntax. To support this transition, we designed and implemented BlockPython. The platform centers on bidirectional translation between blocks and Python and guides learners through four stages: Task Decomposition, Block-Based Practice, Code Challenge, and Extended Interaction. Across these stages, learners progressively establish connections among program structure, runtime behavior, and textual code. During learning, the platform continuously collects process evidence, including block artifacts, code versions, run outcomes, use of support, and dialogue. Deterministic diagnosis, program visualization, and the learning assistant use this evidence to identify different difficulties in computational understanding and Python expression. The rule-based system is responsible for program execution, objective evaluation, and stage control, while the learning assistant uses verified evidence to provide explanations, prompts, and guiding questions. This report describes the design rationale, learning workflow, and process-aware support mechanisms of BlockPython and provides a system-design reference for supporting the transition from block-based to text-based programming and for analyzing learning processes.

AI.tldr: BlockPython is a platform that uses bidirectional block-Python translation with staged learning and process-aware support to help learners transition from block-based to text-based programming.
AI.motivation: The transition from block-based to text-based programming creates a cognitive gap where learners struggle to convert visible program structures into abstract textual expressions in Python syntax, requiring better educational support.
AI.method: Designed BlockPython with four progressive stages: Task Decomposition, Block-Based Practice, Code Challenge, and Extended Interaction. Uses bidirectional translation between blocks and Python, collects process evidence (block artifacts, code versions, run outcomes, etc.), and employs deterministic diagnosis, program visualization, and a learning assistant to identify difficulties.
AI.result: The platform helps learners progressively establish connections among program structure, runtime behavior, and textual code through systematic, evidence-based support mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: BlockPython provides a comprehensive system design reference for supporting the block-to-text programming transition and analyzing learning processes, with its process-aware support mechanisms offering valuable insights for educational tool development.

title: THBKG: A Temporal Biomedical Knowledge Graph for Decision-Aligned Clinical Advancement Prediction
summary: Inadequate target--disease linkage accounts for 40--50\% of Phase~II efficacy failures, so anticipating which programmes will advance would let sponsors back the hypotheses most likely to reach patients. What a programme can be judged on is the evidence that supported its linkage \emph{when it entered the clinic}. No existing biomedical knowledge graph allows that evidence profile to be assembled as of a past date. We present the Temporal Heterogeneous Biomedical Knowledge Graph (THBKG), which describes and predicts therapeutic target--disease links through time: 110,396 entities and 11.1M edges across nineteen relation types, each edge carrying the year its evidence changed, so a pair's profile can be recovered as it stood when its own decision fell due. On this graph we define a decision-aligned benchmark that predicts, for a target--disease pair entering Phase~II, whether it advances to Phase~III on evidence datable before that decision. Graph propagation over the THBKG outranks every direct-evidence reference scored under the same decision-aligned protocol, reaching a relative success of 4.3--4.5 at the top ten pairs per therapeutic area. The gain concentrates on the 72.8\% of pairs with no direct target--disease evidence at their decision point, where a direct-edge model has nothing to read: the encoders still rank five- to sixfold above chance, recovering the signal by propagating over the intervening biology. Adapting a path-based explainer to the decision-time subgraph decomposes each prediction into the evidence landscape behind the hypothesis for explainable prediction. We release the THBKG as a continually updated substrate for studying therapeutic target hypotheses by retrospective validation.

AI.tldr: THBKG is a temporal biomedical knowledge graph that tracks target-disease evidence over time, enabling prediction of Phase II success based on evidence available at decision time.
AI.motivation: 40-50% of Phase II clinical trial failures stem from inadequate target-disease linkage. Existing biomedical knowledge graphs don't allow retrieval of historical evidence profiles as they existed when clinical decisions were made.
AI.method: Created Temporal Heterogeneous Biomedical Knowledge Graph (THBKG) with 110,396 entities and 11.1M edges across 19 relation types, each timestamped with evidence change year. Used graph propagation algorithms to predict Phase II advancement based on evidence available before decision time.
AI.result: THBKG outperforms all direct-evidence references, achieving 4.3-4.5 relative success rate for top 10 pairs per therapeutic area. Even for 72.8% of pairs with no direct evidence at decision time, the model ranks 5-6x above chance by propagating through biological networks.
AI.conclusion: THBKG enables retrospective validation of therapeutic hypotheses by recovering evidence landscapes as they existed historically, providing explainable predictions and helping sponsors identify the most promising targets for clinical advancement.

title: Unified Agent: Managing Interactions across Devices
summary: As capabilities rapidly increase, AI agents can move from running inside one app to acting across a user's devices over time. Yet existing agent systems still fall short in this scenario. This is because observations are scattered across devices and moments, but mainstream systems are not designed around this fact: a single agent that treats devices as tools lacks effective state management for all devices across time, and multi-agent systems coordinate across agents but do not maintain the compact carried state a cross-device, cross-time request needs. We argue that the agent should maintain an effectively designed state that organizes engagement evidence, stated facts, and the standing request in a compact, action-ready form for deciding its action given the current observation. To compare state designs, we construct a benchmark of user-agent interaction across devices and time. We instantiate this principle in Unified Agent, a stateful agent that carries interaction evidence across devices and moments and uses it with the current observation to act. In the default setting, it significantly outperforms our adaptations of four published designs. Across changes in multimodal large language model (MLLM) family, capability, and reasoning effort, it remains ahead of all compared systems, demonstrating that the state-design advantage is robust across MLLM settings. Our code and data will be publicly available on GitHub.

AI.tldr: A stateful AI agent design that maintains compact, action-ready state across devices and time outperforms existing single-agent and multi-agent systems in cross-device scenarios.
AI.motivation: As AI agents become capable of operating across multiple devices over time, existing systems fall short because observations are scattered across devices and moments. Current approaches either use a single agent treating devices as tools (lacking effective state management) or multi-agent systems (which don't maintain compact carried state for cross-device, cross-time requests).
AI.method: The authors propose that agents should maintain an effectively designed state organizing engagement evidence, stated facts, and standing requests in a compact, action-ready form. They construct a benchmark for user-agent interaction across devices and time, and instantiate this principle in Unified Agent - a stateful agent that carries interaction evidence across devices and moments and uses it with current observations to act.
AI.result: Unified Agent significantly outperforms adaptations of four published designs in default settings. The advantage remains robust across changes in multimodal large language model (MLLM) family, capability, and reasoning effort, consistently staying ahead of all compared systems.
AI.conclusion: The state-design advantage is robust across MLLM settings, demonstrating that effectively designed state management is crucial for AI agents operating across devices and time. The proposed Unified Agent provides a promising approach for cross-device, cross-time AI agent systems.

title: Observation-Grounded Self-Predictive Reinforcement Learning for Visual Continuous Control
summary: Sample-efficient policy learning from pixels is a long-standing challenge in reinforcement learning (RL). Recent dynamics-based representation learning methods have significantly improved the sample efficiency of model-free visual RL by learning dynamics-aware representations through auxiliary prediction performed either in latent space (self-prediction) or observation space (observation prediction). However, state-of-the-art methods from both categories still struggle on challenging visual control tasks when training data is limited. We posit that relying on either predictive objective alone may be insufficient. In contrast, observation prediction grounds learned representations in observation-level dynamics, but does not directly regularize the temporal predictability of latent representations over extended horizons. In this paper, we propose Observation-Grounded Self-Predictive Representations (OG-SPR), a model-free visual RL algorithm for continuous control that learns representations that are both temporally predictive in latent space and grounded in observation-level dynamics. OG-SPR incorporates two core auxiliary objectives: multi-step latent self-prediction and next-observation prediction. We empirically show that directly imposing latent self-prediction on the shared representation may over-constrain it and does not necessarily improve performance. To address this issue, OG-SPR introduces two lightweight adapters for latent self-prediction, allowing the shared representation to benefit from temporally predictive signals without being forced to directly satisfy the self-prediction objective. Experiments on 28 visual control tasks from the DeepMind Control Suite show that OG-SPR improves aggregate performance over state-of-the-art self-predictive and observation-predictive RL methods, with particularly pronounced gains in challenging domains such as dog and humanoid.

AI.tldr: OG-SPR combines observation prediction and latent self-prediction with lightweight adapters to learn better visual representations for RL, achieving state-of-the-art performance on challenging continuous control tasks.
AI.motivation: Sample-efficient policy learning from pixels remains challenging. Existing dynamics-based methods using either self-prediction (in latent space) or observation prediction each have limitations: self-prediction may learn representations ungrounded in observations, while observation prediction doesn't regularize long-term temporal predictability of latent representations. Relying on either alone is insufficient for difficult visual control tasks with limited data.
AI.method: OG-SPR (Observation-Grounded Self-Predictive Representations) introduces two core auxiliary objectives: multi-step latent self-prediction and next-observation prediction. To prevent latent self-prediction from over-constraining shared representations, the method uses two lightweight adapters that allow representations to benefit from predictive signals without being forced to directly satisfy self-prediction objectives.
AI.result: Experiments on 28 visual control tasks from DeepMind Control Suite show OG-SPR improves aggregate performance over state-of-the-art self-predictive and observation-predictive RL methods. Gains are particularly pronounced in challenging domains like dog and humanoid control tasks.
AI.conclusion: Combining observation-grounded and self-predictive objectives with careful architectural design (using lightweight adapters) enables learning better representations for visual RL, achieving superior sample efficiency and performance on challenging continuous control tasks.

title: Subliminal Learning is Non-Semantic Distillation
comment: Accepted as spotlight paper for the ICML 2026 Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop
summary: Subliminal Learning (SL) is a surprising type of generalization displayed by modern language models. It allows the transfer of a bias or behavior from a teacher model to a student by distilling from seemingly unrelated or random synthetic data from the teacher. This presents challenges in ensuring AI systems remain predictable and are trained safely, as standard auditing of the input data would not catch the hidden subliminal signal. Here, we investigate several open questions as to the enabling mechanisms and drivers of SL. First is the nature of the process by which biases are encoded in the data. We find that by adding Gaussian noise to the weights of the teacher and student models, the magnitude of subliminal transfer is increased by a factor of 1.9 in Gemma and 1.3 in Llama, suggesting that non-semantic weight structures play a crucial role. We show that steering vectors can be applied to the teacher to produce subliminal data, in addition to prompting and finetuning as used in previous studies. Analysis of the activations of the student models that have been trained on steered and prompted data demonstrates that students inherit not just the semantic meaning of the teacher's bias, but also the type of intervention that was used to apply it: steered students imitate steering vectors, prompted students do not. Additionally, the gradients of steered subliminal data show a linear correlation with the teacher's steering vectors, showing promise for data auditing.
